{{italic title}}

'''''Convergence of Probability Measures''''' 
is a graduate textbook in the field of mathematical [[probability theory]]. 
It was written by [[Patrick Billingsley]] and published by Wiley in 1968. A second edition in 1999 both simplified its treatment of previous topics and updated the book for more recent developments.{{r|schweizer}} The Basic Library List Committee of the [[Mathematical Association of America]] has recommended its inclusion in undergraduate mathematics libraries.{{r|bll}} Readers are expected to already be familiar with both the fundamentals of probability theory and the [[topology]] of [[metric space]]s.{{r|theodorescu}}

The subject [[Convergence of measures|weak convergence of measures]] involves 
rigorous study of how a continuous time (or space) stochastic process arises as a
[[scaling limit]] of a discrete time (or space)  process.
A fundamental example, [[Donsker's theorem]], is convergence of 
rescaled [[random walk]] to [[Wiener process|Brownian motion]]. 
The mathematical theory, combining probability and [[functional analysis]],
was first developed in the 1950s by  [[Anatoliy Skorokhod|Skorokhod]] and [[Yuri Prokhorov|Prokhorov]], but was regarded as a specialized advanced topic. This book's contribution was a self-contained treatment at a useful basic level of abstraction, that of [[Polish space]]. It covers key theory tools such as [[Prokhorov's theorem]] on relative compactness of measures and the [[Càdlàg|Skorokhod space of càdlàg functions]]. The second edition includes
[[Skorokhod's representation theorem]].  Though criticized by [[Richard M. Dudley|Dudley]] for insufficient generality,{{r|dudley}} a reviewer wrote "the subject matter is of great current interest and the exposition is lucid and elegant."{{r|MR}} By being widely accessible it was for many years the standard reference, as evidenced by over 22,000 citations on Google Scholar.  In particular, the subject became a highly valuable tool within burgeoning fields of [[applied probability]] such as [[queueing theory]]{{r|iglehart}} and [[empirical process]] theory in statistics.{{r|shorack}}
